nameStory: The twospot flounder gets its name from the characteristic pair of dark spots that typically appear on its sandy-colored body. Like all flounders, this fish has evolved the remarkable ability to 'flatten' itself against the ocean floor, earning the family their common name from the Old English word meaning 'to founder' or lie flat.
description: The twospot flounder is a fascinating flatfish that spends its life lying sideways on sandy ocean bottoms. This lefteye flounder has both eyes positioned on its left side, allowing it to watch for predators and prey while camouflaged against the seafloor. Most individuals reach about 7 inches in length, though they can grow up to nearly 10 inches. Their flattened, oval-shaped body is perfectly adapted for their bottom-dwelling lifestyle in New England's coastal waters.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Extremely flattened, oval body that feels surprisingly firm and muscular when handled, like a flexible dinner plate with substantial weight

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Two distinctive dark spots on the eyed (left) side that remain visible even when the fish changes color to match the bottom - these spots feel slightly raised to the touch

idTips.label: Eye Position
idTips.description: Both eyes located on the left side of the head, with the top eye often protruding slightly and feeling mobile under gentle pressure

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Long dorsal and anal fins that run almost the entire length of the body, feeling delicate and papery with a slight translucent quality

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Typically 6-7 inches long, fitting comfortably in an adult's palm with a weight that feels substantial for its thinness

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found buried in sand or mud in depths of 30-165 feet, often completely hidden except for the eyes and gill opening

habitat: In New England waters, twospot flounders inhabit sandy and muddy bottoms of the continental shelf, typically at depths between 30 and 165 feet. They prefer areas with fine sediment where they can easily bury themselves, often near the edges of underwater valleys or gentle slopes. These fish are most commonly encountered by offshore anglers and in commercial fishing nets rather than by shore-based observers.

seasonality.spring: Adults may move into slightly shallower waters as temperatures warm. This is when they're most likely to be caught by recreational anglers fishing offshore.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when twospot flounders are actively feeding and most responsive to bait. Water temperatures are optimal for their metabolism and movement.
seasonality.fall: Fish may begin moving to deeper waters as surface temperatures cool. Feeding activity remains high as they prepare for winter.
seasonality.winter: Generally found in deeper, more stable temperature zones. Less active and harder to locate, though still present in New England waters year-round.

funFact: Twospot flounders are born looking like normal fish with eyes on both sides of their head, but as they grow, one eye literally migrates across the top of their skull to join the other eye - a process that takes several weeks and completely restructures their skull bones!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small flounders, but the two prominent dark spots are diagnostic. Remember: 'Two spots, twospot' - while other flounders may have mottled patterns or single spots, the paired spots of the twospot flounder are unmistakable.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'lefteye flounder' refers to which side of the body the eyes migrate to during development, not which side the fish lies on. This can be confusing since the fish actually lies on its right (eyeless) side with its left (eyed) side facing up toward the surface.
compareHints: As the only Bothus species regularly found in New England waters, twospot flounders are distinguished from other local flounders by their specific two-spot pattern and relatively small size. Unlike winter flounder which are righteye flounders, twospot flounders have their eyes on the left side and prefer deeper offshore waters rather than shallow coastal areas.
